title: Ἀγορὰ καὶ ἀοιδός
titleEn: The Assembly and the Minstrel — Odyssey 8.1–96
about: The next morning Alcinous and Odysseus go together to the assembly of the Phaeacians beside the ships. Athena, in the likeness of the king's herald, goes through the town and summons everyone to see the stranger, and she gives Odysseus a greater stature and a wondrous grace, so that he may win the Phaeacians' respect for the trials to come. Alcinous asks for a ship, a crew of fifty-two young men chosen from the people, and then a feast in his house to which the sceptred kings and the singer Demodocus are called. The ship is launched, the feast is prepared, and the blind singer, whom the Muse loved and blinded, is seated and given his lyre. He sings of the quarrel of Odysseus and Achilles, and Odysseus hides his face in his cloak and weeps, unseen by all but Alcinous, who notices his groans and begins to speak.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
ὤρνυτ’ ἄρ’ ἐξ εὐνῆς ἱερὸν μένος Ἀλκινόοιο,
ἂν δ’ ἄρα διογενὴς ὦρτο πτολίπορθος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
up rose from his bed the sacred strength of Alcinous,
and up then rose Zeus-sprung, city-sacking Odysseus.
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, the sacred strength of Alcinous rose from his bed, and Zeus-born Odysseus, the sacker of cities, rose too.
sentences.n: Homer's standing dawn-line opens the part. ὤρνυτ’ is the imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι 'rouse', here 'was rising'. ἱερὸν μένος Ἀλκινόοιο is a periphrasis: 'the sacred strength of Alcinous' stands for Alcinous himself, with a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου). ἂν δ’ … ὦρτο is tmesis: ἀνά stands apart from its verb, and together they are ἀνώρτο 'rose up'. διογενής is 'Zeus-born'. πτολίπορθος 'sacker of cities' is πτολίεθρον / πτόλις 'city' with πέρθω 'sack', a title Odysseus has earned at Troy.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ ἡγεμόνευ’ ἱερὸν μένος Ἀλκινόοιο
Φαιήκων ἀγορήνδ’, ἥ σφιν παρὰ νηυσὶ τέτυκτο.
sentences.l:
And for them led the way the sacred strength of Alcinous
to the Phaeacians’ assembly, which for them beside the ships had been made.
sentences.i: The sacred strength of Alcinous led them to the assembly of the Phaeacians, which had been set up for them beside the ships.
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is a dative in -οισι(ν) and is governed by ἡγεμόνευ’ (ἡγεμόνευε), which takes the dative: 'led the way for them'. ἀγορήνδ’ has the suffix -δε of direction, 'to the assembly' (cf. οἶκόνδε). The relative ἥ is feminine, agreeing with ἀγορήν. σφιν is σφι(ν) 'for them'. τέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω 'make', without augment: 'had been made'.

sentences.t:
ἐλθόντες δὲ καθῖζον ἐπὶ ξεστοῖσι λίθοισι
πλησίον.
sentences.l:
And having come, they sat down upon polished stones
near by.
sentences.i: When they had come, they sat down close by on polished stones.
sentences.n: καθῖζον is the imperfect of καθίζω 'sit down', with no ἐ- augment. ξεστοῖσι λίθοισι is a dative in -οισι(ν): ξεστός is 'smoothed, polished', from ξέω 'scrape, plane', the seats of the assembly. πλησίον is an adverb, 'near', and it ends the sentence in the middle of the line; the next unit starts with the rest of the line.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἀνὰ ἄστυ μετῴχετο Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
εἰδομένη κήρυκι δαΐφρονος Ἀλκινόοιο,
νόστον Ὀδυσσῆι μεγαλήτορι μητιόωσα,
καί ῥα ἑκάστῳ φωτὶ παρισταμένη φάτο μῦθον·
sentences.l:
And she, up through the city, went about, Pallas Athena,
making herself like the herald of wise-minded Alcinous,
planning a homecoming for great-spirited Odysseus,
and, standing beside each man, she spoke a word:
sentences.i: And Pallas Athena went about the city, taking the likeness of the herald of wise-hearted Alcinous, contriving a homecoming for great-spirited Odysseus; and she stood by each man and spoke to him:
sentences.n: ἡ here is a pronoun, 'she'. ἀνὰ ἄστυ is 'up and down through the city'; μετῴχετο is the imperfect of μετοίχομαι 'go among'. εἰδομένη is from εἴδομαι 'make oneself like', and it takes the dative κήρυκι. δαΐφρονος is an old epithet of doubtful meaning: it is read here as 'wise-minded', from the aorist δαῆναι 'learn', but the other ancient explanation, 'battle-minded', from δαΐ 'in battle', is possible. μητιόωσα is a participle with diectasis (Attic μητιῶσα), 'contriving', and Ὀδυσσῆι μεγαλήτορι is a dative, the person for whom she plans. φάτο is the unaugmented ἔφατο 'she spoke'. The colon opens her speech.

sentences.t:
δεῦτ’ ἄγε, Φαιήκων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες,
εἰς ἀγορὴν ἰέναι, ὄφρα ξείνοιο πύθησθε,
ὃς νέον Ἀλκινόοιο δαΐφρονος ἵκετο δῶμα
πόντον ἐπιπλαγχθείς, δέμας ἀθανάτοισιν ὁμοῖος.
sentences.l:
“Hither, come now, leaders and lords of the Phaeacians,
to go to the assembly, that of the stranger you may learn,
who newly of wise-minded Alcinous came to the house,
having been driven-astray over the open-sea, in body like the immortals.”
sentences.i: “Come here, leaders and lords of the Phaeacians, and go to the assembly, to learn about the stranger who has just come to the house of wise-hearted Alcinous, driven astray over the open sea, in body like the immortals.”
sentences.n: Athena, in the herald's likeness, speaks; Murray prints no quotation marks and the Greek has none. δεῦτ’ ἄγε is 'hither, come now' (δεῦτε is the plural of δεῦρο). ἰέναι, the infinitive of εἶμι 'go', is used like an imperative. ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive πύθησθε gives purpose, and πυνθάνομαι takes the genitive of the person one learns about: ξείνοιο, Ionic for ξένου, with -οιο. ἵκετο is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι 'came'; the metre here needs a long ι, and that lengthening is the augment, which the spelling cannot show. ἐπιπλαγχθείς is the aorist passive participle of ἐπιπλάζομαι, from πλάζω 'drive off course': 'having been driven astray'. δέμας is an accusative of respect, 'in body'; ἀθανάτοισιν is a dative in -οισιν governed by ὁμοῖος 'like'.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ὤτρυνε μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἑκάστου.
sentences.l: So having spoken, she roused the strength and the heart of each.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and roused the strength and heart of every man.
sentences.n: ὣς, accented, is 'so, thus' (unaccented ὡς is 'as'); εἰποῦσ’ is the aorist participle of εἶπον, elided, feminine, 'having spoken'. ὤτρυνε is the augmented aorist of ὀτρύνω 'rouse, urge on'. In Homer the augment is optional, so you meet augmented and unaugmented forms side by side. μένος is 'force, strength', θυμός here 'heart'.

sentences.t:
καρπαλίμως δ’ ἔμπληντο βροτῶν ἀγοραί τε καὶ ἕδραι
ἀγρομένων·
sentences.l:
And quickly were filled, of mortals, both the meeting-places and the seats,
of those assembling;
sentences.i: Quickly the meeting-places and the seats were filled with men as they gathered;
sentences.n: ἔμπληντο is the aorist passive of ἐμπίμπλημι 'fill', without augment (ἐν has become ἐμ- before π). καρπαλίμως is an adverb 'swiftly'. ἀγοραί is the plural, 'meeting-places', and ἕδραι are the 'seats'. ἀγρομένων is the genitive plural of the syncopated aorist middle participle of ἀγείρω 'gather', 'of those assembling', and it qualifies βροτῶν.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐθηήσαντο ἰδόντες
υἱὸν Λαέρταο δαΐφρονα·
sentences.l:
And many marvelled, on seeing
the son of Laertes, wise-minded;
sentences.i: and many marvelled at the sight of the wise-hearted son of Laertes;
sentences.n: ἐθηήσαντο is the aorist middle of θηέομαι 'gaze at, marvel at', uncontracted (Attic θεάομαι), with ἰδόντες 'having seen'. Λαέρταο is a genitive in -αο, Attic -ου. δαΐφρονα is the epithet of doubtful meaning already met at line 8: 'wise-minded' is followed, and 'battle-minded' is the other ancient guess.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ Ἀθήνη
θεσπεσίην κατέχευε χάριν κεφαλῇ τε καὶ ὤμοις
καί μιν μακρότερον καὶ πάσσονα θῆκεν ἰδέσθαι,
sentences.l:
and upon him Athena
a wondrous grace poured-down, on head and shoulders,
and made him taller and stouter to look upon,
sentences.i: and upon him Athena shed a wondrous grace, on head and shoulders, and made him taller and stouter to look upon,
sentences.n: τῷ is a pronoun, 'upon him'. θεσπεσίην, 'wondrous', agrees with χάριν 'grace'. κατέχευε is the aorist of καταχέω 'pour down over'. κεφαλῇ τε καὶ ὤμοις gives the place, with a dative in -οις. μακρότερον and πάσσονα are comparatives of μακρός 'tall' and παχύς 'thick, stout', with πάσσων the epic form; ἰδέσθαι is the aorist infinitive 'to look upon'.

sentences.t:
ὥς κεν Φαιήκεσσι φίλος πάντεσσι γένοιτο
δεινός τ’ αἰδοῖός τε καὶ ἐκτελέσειεν ἀέθλους
πολλούς, τοὺς Φαίηκες ἐπειρήσαντ’ Ὀδυσῆος.
sentences.l:
so that to all the Phaeacians dear he might become,
and dread and revered, and might bring to completion the contests
many, which the Phaeacians made trial of Odysseus.
sentences.i: so that he might be dear to all the Phaeacians, and dread and revered, and might carry through the many contests with which the Phaeacians tried Odysseus.
sentences.n: ὥς κεν with the optative γένοιτο and ἐκτελέσειεν gives purpose: 'so that he might become'. κε(ν) is the epic form of ἄν. Φαιήκεσσι and πάντεσσι are datives in -εσσι(ν). δεινός is 'dread', that is, inspiring awe and fear together. ἐπειρήσαντ’ is the aorist middle of πειράομαι 'make trial of', which takes the genitive Ὀδυσῆος for the person tried, while τοὺς (referring to ἀέθλους) is an accusative of the trial made: 'the contests with which they tried Odysseus' (one σ, where Ὀδυσσῆος has two: the metre decides).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἤγερθεν ὁμηγερέες τ’ ἐγένοντο,
τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀλκίνοος ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε·
sentences.l:
But when they were gathered and assembled-together had become,
to them Alcinous addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: When they had gathered and were all assembled, Alcinous addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: ῥ’ is the particle ῥα 'then'. ἤγερθεν is the aorist passive of ἀγείρω 'gather', with -θεν where Attic has -θησαν. ὁμηγερέες is 'gathered together'. ἀγορήσατο is the aorist of ἀγοράομαι 'address an assembly', and μετέειπε is 'spoke among them', the epic form of μετεῖπε. The two verbs make a standing speech-introduction, and the colon opens Alcinous' speech.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτε, Φαιήκων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες,
ὄφρ’ εἴπω τά με θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι κελεύει.
sentences.l:
“Hear me, leaders and lords of the Phaeacians,
that I may say what my heart in my breast bids.
sentences.i: “Hear me, leaders and lords of the Phaeacians, so that I may say what the heart in my breast bids me say.
sentences.n: Alcinous speaks, again without marks in the Greek. κέκλυτε is a reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω 'hear': 'hear me'. ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες is 'leaders and lords', ἠδέ being the epic 'and'. ὄφρ’ εἴπω is ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive, 'that I may say'. τά is a relative, 'what', the object of εἴπω, and με is the person bidden, the object of κελεύει: 'what … bids me say'. στήθεσσι is a dative in -εσσι, plural for the one chest, the seat of the θυμός 'heart'.

sentences.t:
ξεῖνος ὅδ’, οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅς τις, ἀλώμενος ἵκετ’ ἐμὸν δῶ,
ἠὲ πρὸς ἠοίων ἦ ἑσπερίων ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.l:
This stranger, I know not who, wandering, has come to my house,
either from men of the dawn or from men of the evening;
sentences.i: This stranger, I do not know who he is, has come wandering to my house, whether from the men of the dawn or from the men of the evening;
sentences.n: ξεῖνος is the Ionic form of ξένος, 'stranger, guest'. ὅδ’ is ὅδε 'this'. οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅς τις is 'I do not know who', the indirect question. ἀλώμενος is the participle of ἀλάομαι 'wander', and ἵκετ’ is ἵκετο, the aorist of ἱκνέομαι, elided; the metre needs its ι long, and that lengthening is the augment, which the spelling cannot show. δῶ is δῶμα 'house' cut short. ἠοίων and ἑσπερίων are 'of the dawn' and 'of the evening', that is, the peoples of the sunrise and the sunset: he may come from anywhere in the world. πρός with the genitive means 'from the side of'.

sentences.t: πομπὴν δ’ ὀτρύνει, καὶ λίσσεται ἔμπεδον εἶναι.
sentences.l: and he urges an escort, and entreats that it be steadfast.
sentences.i: He presses for an escort, and begs that it be a sure one.
sentences.n: πομπή is 'escort', the sending of a guest on his way, which for the Phaeacians means the ship that carries him home. ὀτρύνει is 'urges on, hastens', and its object is πομπήν, as ἐποτρυνώμεθα takes πομπήν in the next line. λίσσεται is 'entreats', and ἔμπεδον is 'firm, steady', a neuter used as an adverb with εἶναι (the escort being understood as its subject): 'that it be firm'.

sentences.t: ἡμεῖς δ’, ὡς τὸ πάρος περ, ἐποτρυνώμεθα πομπήν.
sentences.l: But we, as before indeed, let us speed the escort.
sentences.i: But let us, as we have done before, speed the escort.
sentences.n: ἐποτρυνώμεθα is a hortatory subjunctive, 'let us speed on'. ἡμεῖς is emphatic, set against the stranger of the last three lines. ὡς τὸ πάρος περ is 'as before indeed', τὸ πάρος being a phrase for 'formerly', with περ adding force.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδέ τις ἄλλος, ὅτις κ’ ἐμὰ δώμαθ’ ἵκηται,
ἐνθάδ’ ὀδυρόμενος δηρὸν μένει εἵνεκα πομπῆς.
sentences.l:
For not even any other, whoever may come to my house,
here lamenting stays long on account of an escort.
sentences.i: For no other man either, whoever may come to my house, stays on here long, lamenting, because of an escort.
sentences.n: οὐδὲ … οὐδέ … is 'not even, not any', two negatives that strengthen each other. ὅτις κ’ … ἵκηται is a general relative clause: ὅτις is ὅστις, κ’ is κε(ν), and ἵκηται is the aorist subjunctive, 'whoever may come'. δώμαθ’ is δώματα, elided; the plural stands for the single house. ὀδυρόμενος is 'lamenting'. εἵνεκα is the epic form of ἕνεκα 'on account of', here 'because he has no escort'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῆα μέλαιναν ἐρύσσομεν εἰς ἅλα δῖαν
πρωτόπλοον, κούρω δὲ δύω καὶ πεντήκοντα
κρινάσθων κατὰ δῆμον, ὅσοι πάρος εἰσὶν ἄριστοι.
sentences.l:
But come, a black ship let us drag down into the heavenly brine,
first-voyaging, and two youths and fifty
let them choose out through the people, those who before are best.
sentences.i: But come, let us drag a black ship down into the heavenly brine, one on her first voyage, and let them choose out two and fifty youths from among the people, those who have been the best until now.
sentences.n: ἐρύσσομεν is a subjunctive with a short vowel (for ἐρύσσωμεν), used as 'let us drag down'. ἅλα δῖαν is 'the heavenly brine', with δῖος 'heavenly' kept for the sea. πρωτόπλοον, from πρῶτος and πλόος 'voyage', is 'making its first voyage', that is, a new ship. κούρω is a dual form, as is κρινθέντε at 48, though the number is fifty-two: the dual seems to be drawn in by δύω 'two'. κρινάσθων is the third plural imperative middle of κρίνω 'pick out', 'let them choose'. κατὰ δῆμον is 'through the people'. πάρος is 'before, until now'.

sentences.t:
δησάμενοι δ’ ἐὺ πάντες ἐπὶ κληῖσιν ἐρετμὰ
ἔκβητ’·
sentences.l:
And having bound well, all of you, the oars upon the thole-pins,
come out;
sentences.i: Bind the oars well to the thole-pins, all of you, and come ashore;
sentences.n: δησάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of δέω 'bind, lash', 'having made fast'. ἐὺ is εὖ 'well'. κληῖσιν is a dative plural in -ῖσιν, and 'thole-pins' is the usual guess for it, the pegs to which the oars are lashed. ἐρετμά is 'oars'. ἔκβητ’ is the aorist imperative of ἐκβαίνω 'step out', here out of the ship. The participle plus imperative means 'make the oars fast, then come out'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα θοὴν ἀλεγύνετε δαῖτα
ἡμέτερόνδ’ ἐλθόντες·
sentences.l:
and then a swift feast see to
having come to our house;
sentences.i: and then come to our house and see to a swift feast;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα is 'and then', where Attic prose would use δέ. ἀλεγύνετε is 'see to, take care of', and θοήν is 'swift': the feast is to be got ready quickly. ἡμέτερόνδ’ has the suffix -δε of direction, 'to our house', with the noun understood.

sentences.t: ἐγὼ δ’ ἐὺ πᾶσι παρέξω.
sentences.l: and I will furnish well for all.
sentences.i: and I will provide well for everyone.
sentences.n: ἐγώ is emphatic: the king will supply the food. παρέξω is the future of παρέχω 'furnish, supply', and ἐὺ … πᾶσι is 'well for all'.

sentences.t: κούροισιν μὲν ταῦτ’ ἐπιτέλλομαι·
sentences.l: To the youths, indeed, these things I enjoin;
sentences.i: These are my orders to the young men;
sentences.n: κούροισιν is a dative in -οισιν; κοῦρος is the Ionic form of κόρος, 'young man'. ἐπιτέλλομαι is 'lay a charge on, enjoin'. μέν looks forward to the αὐτάρ of the next unit: 'to the young men … but the rest of you …'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ οἱ ἄλλοι
σκηπτοῦχοι βασιλῆες ἐμὰ πρὸς δώματα καλὰ
ἔρχεσθ’, ὄφρα ξεῖνον ἐνὶ μεγάροισι φιλέωμεν,
μηδέ τις ἀρνείσθω.
sentences.l:
but the rest of you,
sceptre-bearing kings, to my fair house,
come, that the stranger in the halls we may entertain,
and let no one refuse.
sentences.i: and the rest of you, the sceptred kings, come to my fair house, so that we may entertain the stranger in the halls, and let no one refuse.
sentences.n: οἱ ἄλλοι is 'the others'. σκηπτοῦχοι βασιλῆες is 'sceptre-bearing kings', the lords of the Phaeacians, who each carry the staff of office. δώματα is again a plural for one house. ἔρχεσθ’ is the imperative ἔρχεσθε 'come'. ὄφρα with the subjunctive φιλέωμεν gives purpose; φιλέωμεν is uncontracted, 'treat as a friend, entertain'. ἀρνείσθω is the third singular imperative, 'let him refuse'.

sentences.t:
καλέσασθε δὲ θεῖον ἀοιδὸν
Δημόδοκον·
sentences.l:
And call the divine minstrel,
Demodocus;
sentences.i: And summon the divine minstrel, Demodocus;
sentences.n: καλέσασθε is the aorist imperative middle of καλέω 'summon (for ourselves)'. θεῖον ἀοιδόν is 'the divine minstrel', θεῖος being 'divine' and the ἀοιδός the singer of the heroic songs. The name Δημόδοκος, put last in the sentence, is the first news of who the singer is.

sentences.t:
τῷ γάρ ῥα θεὸς πέρι δῶκεν ἀοιδὴν
τέρπειν, ὅππῃ θυμὸς ἐποτρύνῃσιν ἀείδειν.
sentences.l:
for to him a god beyond others gave song
to delight with, in whatever way his heart may urge him to sing.”
sentences.i: for to him, above all others, a god gave the gift of song, to give delight in whatever way his heart urges him to sing.”
sentences.n: τῷ is a pronoun, 'to him'. ῥα is a particle, 'you see'. πέρι is here an adverb, 'exceedingly, beyond others'. δῶκεν is the aorist of δίδωμι, and τέρπειν is an infinitive of purpose, 'to delight'. ὅππῃ is 'in whatever way'. ἐποτρύνῃσιν is a subjunctive in -ῃσιν, the old third singular ending, in a general clause: 'however his heart may urge'. The closing mark ends Alcinous' speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἡγήσατο, τοὶ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο
σκηπτοῦχοι·
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, he led the way, and they together followed,
the sceptre-bearers;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and led the way, and they followed along together, the sceptre-bearers;
sentences.n: φωνήσας is the aorist participle of φωνέω 'speak', and ἡγήσατο the aorist of ἡγέομαι 'lead the way'. τοί is the epic pronoun 'they' (Attic οἱ). ἕποντο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι 'follow', without augment. σκηπτοῦχοι, 'sceptre-bearers', stands after the verb in apposition to τοί.

sentences.t: κῆρυξ δὲ μετῴχετο θεῖον ἀοιδόν.
sentences.l: and the herald went after the divine minstrel.
sentences.i: while the herald went to fetch the divine minstrel.
sentences.n: μετῴχετο is the imperfect of μετοίχομαι, which meant 'went about' at line 7 with ἀνά, and here takes an object, 'went after, went in quest of'. θεῖον ἀοιδόν is the same 'divine minstrel' as at 43.

sentences.t:
κούρω δὲ κρινθέντε δύω καὶ πεντήκοντα
βήτην, ὡς ἐκέλευσ’, ἐπὶ θῖν’ ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο.
sentences.l:
And the youths, having been chosen, two and fifty,
went, as he had ordered, to the shore of the unharvested salt-sea.
sentences.i: And the two and fifty young men who had been chosen went, as he had ordered, to the shore of the sea that yields no harvest.
sentences.n: κούρω and κρινθέντε are dual forms (see line 35) and βήτην is the dual of the aorist of βαίνω, 'the two went', all agreeing with a company of fifty-two. ὡς ἐκέλευσ’ is 'as he had ordered'. θῖνα is the accusative of θίς 'beach, shore'. ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο is a genitive in -οιο. ἀτρύγετος is an old epithet whose meaning is unknown: 'unharvested, barren', from ἀ- and τρυγάω 'harvest', is the ancient guess, and 'unresting' another.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἐπὶ νῆα κατήλυθον ἠδὲ θάλασσαν,
νῆα μὲν οἵ γε μέλαιναν ἁλὸς βένθοσδε ἔρυσσαν,
sentences.l:
But when then they had come down to the ship and the sea,
the ship, then, they, the black one, into the depths of the sea drew,
sentences.i: And when they had come down to the ship and the sea, they drew the black ship down into the depths of the sea;
sentences.n: κατήλυθον is the aorist of κατέρχομαι 'come down', in the epic -ήλυθον form. ῥ’ is ῥα. The sentence runs on to line 54, five lines in all, and the unit is cut at the comma so that no unit runs past four lines. βένθοσδε is 'to the depths', βένθος being the poetic form of βάθος, with the suffix -σδε of direction. ἔρυσσαν is the aorist of ἐρύω 'drag', with no augment; οἵ γε is 'they', with emphasis. μὲν looks forward to the ἐν δ’ of the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἱστόν τ’ ἐτίθεντο καὶ ἱστία νηὶ μελαίνῃ,
ἠρτύναντο δ’ ἐρετμὰ τροποῖς ἐν δερματίνοισι,
πάντα κατὰ μοῖραν, ἀνά θ’ ἱστία λευκὰ πέτασσαν.
sentences.l:
and in it they set the mast and the sails, in the black ship,
and they fitted the oars into the leathern thongs,
all according to what is fitting, and they spread the white sails.
sentences.i: and set the mast and sails in the black ship, fitted the oars into their leather thongs, everything as was fitting, and spread the white sails.
sentences.n: ἐν δ’ … ἐτίθεντο is tmesis (ἐντίθεντο 'put in'), and ἀνά … πέτασσαν is tmesis again, ἀναπετάννυμι 'spread out'. ἠρτύναντο is the aorist middle of ἀρτύνω 'fit, make ready'. τροποῖς … δερματίνοισι, 'in leathern thongs', are the leather loops that held each oar to its pin; the archive prints the adjective without the final ν. κατὰ μοῖραν is 'in due measure, as is fitting'.

sentences.t: ὑψοῦ δ’ ἐν νοτίῳ τήν γ’ ὥρμισαν·
sentences.l: And high up, in the water, they moored it;
sentences.i: and moored her high, in the water;
sentences.n: ὑψοῦ is 'on high' and ἐν νοτίῳ is 'in the wet', νότιος being 'wet, watery' (or perhaps 'of the south wind'). The exact picture is not clear: the ship rides at her mooring out on the water. τήν γ’ is 'her', the ship, feminine. ὥρμισαν is the aorist of ὁρμίζω 'bring to moorings'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
βάν ῥ’ ἴμεν Ἀλκινόοιο δαΐφρονος ἐς μέγα δῶμα.
sentences.l:
and then
they set out to go to the great house of wise-minded Alcinous.
sentences.i: and then they set out for the great house of wise-hearted Alcinous.
sentences.n: βάν ῥ’ ἴμεν is a standing phrase: βάν is the unaugmented third plural aorist of βαίνω 'they went', ῥ’ is ῥα, and ἴμεν is the infinitive 'to go' in its epic -μεν form (Attic ἰέναι): 'they set out to go'. Ἀλκινόοιο δαΐφρονος is a genitive in -οιο with the epithet of uncertain sense (see line 8).

sentences.t:
πλῆντο δ’ ἄρ’ αἴθουσαί τε καὶ ἕρκεα καὶ δόμοι ἀνδρῶν
ἀγρομένων·
sentences.l:
And were filled then the porticoes and the courts and the houses of men,
of those assembling;
sentences.i: Then the porticoes, the courtyards and the houses were filled with the men who gathered;
sentences.n: πλῆντο is the unaugmented aorist passive of πίμπλημι, as ἔμπληντο was at 16. αἴθουσαι are roofed porticoes, ἕρκεα are 'enclosures, courts', and δόμοι are 'houses'. ἀνδρῶν ἀγρομένων is 'of men assembling', echoing ἀγρομένων at line 17.

sentences.t: πολλοὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔσαν, νέοι ἠδὲ παλαιοί.
sentences.l: And many they were, young and old.
sentences.i: There were many of them, both young and old.
sentences.n: ἔσαν is the epic ἦσαν 'they were'. νέοι ἠδὲ παλαιοί is 'young and old', a pairing that means everyone.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀλκίνοος δυοκαίδεκα μῆλ’ ἱέρευσεν,
ὀκτὼ δ’ ἀργιόδοντας ὕας, δύο δ’ εἰλίποδας βοῦς·
sentences.l:
And for them Alcinous twelve sheep slaughtered,
and eight white-toothed pigs, and two rolling-gaited cattle;
sentences.i: For them Alcinous slaughtered twelve sheep, eight white-toothed pigs, and two cattle of rolling gait;
sentences.n: δυοκαίδεκα is 'twelve', two and ten. ἱέρευσεν is the aorist of ἱερεύω 'slaughter for sacrifice', which here is also the preparation of the meal. μῆλα are sheep, ἀργιόδοντας ὕας are 'white-toothed pigs' (that is, boars with white tusks), and εἰλίποδας is 'of rolling gait', from εἰλέω 'roll' and πούς: the cattle sway as they walk.

sentences.t: τοὺς δέρον ἀμφί θ’ ἕπον, τετύκοντό τε δαῖτ’ ἐρατεινήν.
sentences.l: These they flayed, and dressed, and prepared a lovely feast.
sentences.i: They flayed them and dressed the carcasses, and prepared a lovely feast.
sentences.n: τοὺς is a pronoun, 'them'. δέρον is the imperfect of δέρω 'flay', without augment. ἀμφί θ’ ἕπον is tmesis: ἀμφὶ … ἕπον is ἀμφέπω 'busy oneself about, tend', here 'dressed'. τετύκοντο is the reduplicated aorist middle of τεύχω 'make, prepare', and ἐρατεινήν is 'lovely'.

sentences.t:
κῆρυξ δ’ ἐγγύθεν ἦλθεν ἄγων ἐρίηρον ἀοιδόν,
τὸν πέρι μοῦσ’ ἐφίλησε, δίδου δ’ ἀγαθόν τε κακόν τε·
sentences.l:
And the herald from close by came, leading the trusty minstrel,
whom beyond others the Muse loved, and gave both good and evil;
sentences.i: The herald came from close by, leading the trusty minstrel, whom the Muse loved above all others, and gave him both good and evil;
sentences.n: ἐγγύθεν is 'from close by'. ἐρίηρος is 'trusty' (the first part is an intensive, and the exact origin of the word is unclear). τόν is a relative pronoun, 'whom', and πέρι is an adverb, 'above all others'. δίδου is the unaugmented imperfect of δίδωμι 'she gave'. ἀγαθόν τε κακόν τε is 'both good and evil', and the next line says what each was.

sentences.t: ὀφθαλμῶν μὲν ἄμερσε, δίδου δ’ ἡδεῖαν ἀοιδήν.
sentences.l: Of his eyes she deprived him, but gave him sweet song.
sentences.i: She took his sight from him, but gave him sweet song.
sentences.n: ὀφθαλμῶν is a genitive with ἄμερσε, from ἀμέρδω 'deprive', which takes the genitive of what is taken away. μὲν … δέ sets the loss against the gift, and δίδου is again the imperfect 'she gave'.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄρα Ποντόνοος θῆκε θρόνον ἀργυρόηλον
μέσσῳ δαιτυμόνων, πρὸς κίονα μακρὸν ἐρείσας·
sentences.l:
And for him Pontonous set a silver-studded chair
in the middle of the feasters, having propped it against a tall pillar;
sentences.i: And for him Pontonous set a silver-studded chair in the middle of the feasters, propping it against a tall pillar;
sentences.n: τῷ is a pronoun, 'for him'. Ποντόνοος is the herald's name; he is presumably the κῆρυξ of line 62 and 69. ἀργυρόηλον is 'silver-studded', from ἦλος 'nail, stud'. μέσσῳ is 'in the middle' (the doubled σ is epic) with the genitive δαιτυμόνων 'of the feasters'. ἐρείσας is the aorist participle of ἐρείδω 'prop, lean'.

sentences.t:
κὰδ δ’ ἐκ πασσαλόφι κρέμασεν φόρμιγγα λίγειαν
αὐτοῦ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς καὶ ἐπέφραδε χερσὶν ἑλέσθαι
κῆρυξ·
sentences.i: The herald hung the clear-sounding lyre from a peg right above his head, and pointed it out for him to take in his hands;
sentences.n: κὰδ δ’ … κρέμασεν is tmesis: κὰδ is κατά before δ, 'hung down'. ἐκ πασσαλόφι has the suffix -φι, which here gives the place, 'from a peg'. λίγειαν is the feminine of λιγύς 'clear-sounding'. ἐπέφραδε is the reduplicated aorist of φράζω 'point out, show', and ἑλέσθαι is the aorist infinitive middle 'to take'; the blind man has to be told where the lyre hangs. αὐτοῦ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς is 'right above his head'. κῆρυξ, the subject, is held back to the end.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δ’ ἐτίθει κάνεον καλήν τε τράπεζαν,
πὰρ δὲ δέπας οἴνοιο, πιεῖν ὅτε θυμὸς ἀνώγοι.
sentences.l:
and beside him he set a basket and a fair table,
and beside it a cup of wine, to drink whenever his heart bade.
sentences.i: Beside him he set a basket and a fair table, and beside it a cup of wine, to drink whenever his heart bade him.
sentences.n: πάρ is παρά used as an adverb, 'beside'; ἐτίθει is the imperfect of τίθημι. κάνεον is 'basket', here the bread-basket. πιεῖν is the aorist infinitive 'to drink'. ὅτε with the optative ἀνώγοι is a general clause of repeated action, 'whenever his heart should bid him'.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον.
sentences.l: And they to the good things ready and set before them put out their hands.
sentences.i: And they put out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
sentences.n: This is the poem's stock line for the beginning of a meal. οἱ is a pronoun, 'they'. ὀνείαθ’ is ὀνείατα, 'good things, food', and προκείμενα is 'set before them'. ἴαλλον is the imperfect of ἰάλλω 'send out', without augment.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
μοῦσ’ ἄρ’ ἀοιδὸν ἀνῆκεν ἀειδέμεναι κλέα ἀνδρῶν,
οἴμης τῆς τότ’ ἄρα κλέος οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἵκανε,
νεῖκος Ὀδυσσῆος καὶ Πηλεΐδεω Ἀχιλῆος,
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
the Muse impelled the minstrel to sing the glories of men,
of a lay whose fame then reached the wide sky,
the strife of Odysseus and of Peleus’ son Achilles,
sentences.i: But when they had put from them the desire for drink and food, the Muse moved the minstrel to sing the glories of men, a lay whose fame then reached the wide sky: the strife of Odysseus and Achilles, son of Peleus,
sentences.n: The first line is another stock line, the close of a meal. ἔρον is ἔρος 'desire', the object of ἕντο, the aorist middle of ἵημι 'send away'; ἐξ … ἕντο is tmesis (ἐξέντο 'put away from themselves'). ἀνῆκεν is 'impelled, set on', and ἀειδέμεναι is an infinitive in -μεναι, Attic ᾄδειν. κλέα ἀνδρῶν is 'the glories of men', the heroic songs. τῆς is the relative, 'of which' ('whose' in the English); οἴμης is a genitive, 'of a lay'; νεῖκος, 'strife', is accusative, in apposition to κλέα ἀνδρῶν, and says what the lay was. Πηλεΐδεω is a genitive with -εω for -ου, 'of Peleus’ son', and Ὀδυσσῆος is the Ionic genitive of Ὀδυσσεύς. εὐρὺν οὐρανόν is 'the wide sky'.

sentences.t:
ὥς ποτε δηρίσαντο θεῶν ἐν δαιτὶ θαλείῃ
ἐκπάγλοις ἐπέεσσιν, ἄναξ δ’ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων
χαῖρε νόῳ, ὅ τ’ ἄριστοι Ἀχαιῶν δηριόωντο.
sentences.l:
how once they quarrelled at the gods’ abundant feast
with terrible words, and the lord of men, Agamemnon,
rejoiced in mind, that the best of the Achaeans were quarrelling.
sentences.i: how once they quarrelled at the gods’ abundant feast with terrible words, and Agamemnon, lord of men, was glad in mind that the best of the Achaeans were quarrelling.
sentences.n: ὥς ποτε is 'how once', the content of the song. δηρίσαντο is the aorist of δηριάομαι 'contend', and δηριόωντο is the imperfect with diectasis (Attic ἐδηριῶντο). δαιτὶ θαλείῃ is 'abundant feast', δαίς being the feast and θαλείῃ its dative epithet. ἐκπάγλοις is 'terrible'. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν is 'lord of men', the title given to Agamemnon. χαῖρε νόῳ is 'was glad in mind', and ὅ τ’ is ὅ τε, 'that'. Ἀχαιῶν is a partitive genitive after ἄριστοι.

sentences.t:
ὣς γάρ οἱ χρείων μυθήσατο Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων
Πυθοῖ ἐν ἠγαθέῃ, ὅθ’ ὑπέρβη λάινον οὐδὸν
χρησόμενος·
sentences.i: For so Phoebus Apollo had spoken to him in prophecy, in holy Pytho, when he crossed the stone threshold to consult the oracle;
sentences.n: οἱ is 'to him', that is Agamemnon, and the ὅθ’ clause has no named subject: 'he', Agamemnon, is understood. χρείων is most likely a participle, 'giving oracles', from χράω; the form is not certain. Πυθοῖ is a locative dative, 'at Pytho', the old name of Delphi, and ἠγαθέῃ is 'holy'. ὑπέρβη is the unaugmented aorist of ὑπερβαίνω 'step over'. λάινον is 'of stone'. χρησόμενος is the future participle of χράομαι 'consult an oracle', giving the purpose.

sentences.t:
τότε γάρ ῥα κυλίνδετο πήματος ἀρχὴ
Τρωσί τε καὶ Δαναοῖσι Διὸς μεγάλου διὰ βουλάς.
sentences.l:
for then was rolling the beginning of woe
for Trojans and for Danaans, through the counsels of great Zeus.
sentences.i: for then the beginning of woe was rolling on for Trojans and Greeks alike, through the counsels of great Zeus.
sentences.n: κυλίνδετο is the imperfect passive of κυλίνδω 'roll': trouble is a stone set rolling. πήματος is 'of woe' (πῆμα). Δαναοῖσι is a dative in -οισι(ν), and Δαναοί is one of Homer's names for the Greeks. Διὸς μεγάλου διὰ βουλάς is 'through the counsels of great Zeus', διά with the accusative: 'by reason of'. The phrase links Agamemnon's oracle to the plan of Zeus.

sentences.t: ταῦτ’ ἄρ’ ἀοιδὸς ἄειδε περικλυτός·
sentences.l: These things then the minstrel was singing, far-famed;
sentences.i: These were the things the far-famed minstrel sang;
sentences.n: ταῦτ’ is the neuter plural 'these things', looking back to the song just told. ἄειδε is the imperfect of ἀείδω, uncontracted (Attic ᾖδε). περικλυτός is 'far-famed', περι- being intensive.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
πορφύρεον μέγα φᾶρος ἑλὼν χερσὶ στιβαρῇσι
κὰκ κεφαλῆς εἴρυσσε, κάλυψε δὲ καλὰ πρόσωπα·
sentences.i: but Odysseus took his great purple cloak in his sturdy hands, drew it down from his head, and covered his fair face;
sentences.n: The song moves Odysseus, who is still unrecognised. φᾶρος is a man's 'cloak'. ἑλών is the aorist participle of αἱρέω, 'having taken', and χερσὶ στιβαρῇσι is a dative in -ῃσι, 'in sturdy hands'. κὰκ κεφαλῆς is κατὰ κεφαλῆς, 'down from his head', with the final consonant assimilated. εἴρυσσε is the aorist of ἐρύω 'draw'; its ει- is the augment (the verb began with a digamma), unlike ἔρυσσαν at line 51. πρόσωπα is a plural for one face.

sentences.t: αἴδετο γὰρ Φαίηκας ὑπ’ ὀφρύσι δάκρυα λείβων.
sentences.l: for he felt shame before the Phaeacians, under his brows tears pouring.
sentences.i: for he felt shame before the Phaeacians as he poured out his tears under his brows.
sentences.n: αἴδετο is the imperfect of αἰδέομαι 'feel shame before, respect', with the accusative Φαίηκας. ὑπ’ ὀφρύσι is 'under his brows'. δάκρυα λείβων is 'pouring out tears', from λείβω 'pour, let fall'; it recurs at 93.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ὅτε λήξειεν ἀείδων θεῖος ἀοιδός,
δάκρυ ὀμορξάμενος κεφαλῆς ἄπο φᾶρος ἕλεσκε
καὶ δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον ἑλὼν σπείσασκε θεοῖσιν·
sentences.i: Indeed, whenever the divine minstrel stopped singing, he would wipe away his tears, take the cloak from his head, and, taking a double cup, pour libations to the gods;
sentences.n: ἦ τοι is 'indeed, truly'. ὅτε with the optative λήξειεν is a general clause, 'whenever he ceased'. ἕλεσκε and σπείσασκε are iterative forms with the suffix -σκ-, 'he would take', 'he would pour': the scene is repeated. ὀμορξάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ὀμόργνυμι 'wipe away'. δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον is 'double cup', a phrase of disputed sense ('two-handled' is the other guess).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅτ’ ἂψ ἄρχοιτο καὶ ὀτρύνειαν ἀείδειν
Φαιήκων οἱ ἄριστοι, ἐπεὶ τέρποντ’ ἐπέεσσιν,
ἂψ Ὀδυσεὺς κατὰ κρᾶτα καλυψάμενος γοάασκεν.
sentences.l:
but whenever again he began, and urged him to sing
the best of the Phaeacians, since they delighted in the words,
again Odysseus, over his head having covered himself, would groan.
sentences.i: but whenever he began again, and the best of the Phaeacians urged him to sing, since they took pleasure in his words, Odysseus would cover his head again and groan.
sentences.n: ἂψ ἄρχοιτο is 'he began again'; ὀτρύνειαν is the third plural optative, 'they urged him on', with the singer left unsaid. οἱ ἄριστοι is 'the best', the nobles, οἱ being the article. τέρποντ’ is τέρποντο 'they took pleasure', with the dative ἐπέεσσιν 'in his words'. κατὰ κρᾶτα is 'down over his head', and γοάασκεν is an iterative imperfect of γοάω 'wail, groan'. Ὀδυσεύς has one σ, where Ὀδυσσεύς at 83 has two: the metre decides.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλους μὲν πάντας ἐλάνθανε δάκρυα λείβων,
Ἀλκίνοος δέ μιν οἶος ἐπεφράσατ’ ἠδ’ ἐνόησεν
ἥμενος ἄγχ’ αὐτοῦ, βαρὺ δὲ στενάχοντος ἄκουσεν.
sentences.l:
Then all the others he escaped, tears pouring,
but Alcinous, him alone, noticed and perceived,
sitting near him, and heavily groaning he heard.
sentences.i: He escaped the notice of all the others as he poured out his tears, but Alcinous alone noticed him and understood, sitting close beside him, and heard him groaning heavily.
sentences.n: ἐλάνθανε is the imperfect of λανθάνω 'escape the notice of', with the accusative ἄλλους … πάντας. μιν is the epic 'him'. ἐπεφράσατ’ is the aorist middle of ἐπιφράζομαι 'notice', and ἐνόησεν is 'perceived, understood'. ἥμενος is the participle of ἧμαι 'sit'. βαρύ is the neuter used as an adverb, 'heavily'. ἄκουσεν takes the genitive στενάχοντος, since verbs of hearing take the genitive of the one heard.

sentences.t: αἶψα δὲ Φαιήκεσσι φιληρέτμοισι μετηύδα·
sentences.l: And at once among the oar-loving Phaeacians he spoke:
sentences.i: And at once he spoke among the oar-loving Phaeacians:
sentences.n: αἶψα is 'at once'. μετηύδα is the imperfect of μεταυδάω 'speak among', with the dative Φαιήκεσσι. φιληρέτμοισι is a dative in -οισι(ν), 'oar-loving'. The speaker is Alcinous, and what he says follows.
